<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p04" data-practice-set="P04" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p04-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> Before contracting, buyers offer a price based on average quality, causing high-quality sellers with privately known quality to withdraw. After signing and receiving payment, a seller can reduce unobserved effort, lowering the buyer&#x27;s service quality. Which pair identifies the two information problems?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-01-a" name="p04-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Adverse selection; moral hazard</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-01-b" name="p04-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Coordination failure; payoff dominance</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-01-c" name="p04-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Reciprocity; conditional cooperation</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-01-d" name="p04-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Moral hazard; adverse selection</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-01-e" name="p04-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Risk dominance; common knowledge</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> Two teams cooperate internally but resist sharing resources across teams. Which intervention most directly targets the narrow boundary of cooperation?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-02-a" name="p04-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> A ranking rewarding only superiority over the other team</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-02-b" name="p04-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Separate tasks with no need for interteam contact</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-02-c" name="p04-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A reminder that all members of each team think alike</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-02-d" name="p04-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> A shared task requiring contributions from both teams to succeed</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-02-e" name="p04-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> More resources for the existing within-team competition</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> Team members have unique evidence but fear that public disagreement will look disloyal. Which combined procedure most directly addresses both problems?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-03-a" name="p04-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Collect independent evidence privately, then discuss it under explicit protection for dissent.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-03-b" name="p04-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Record only the final unanimous statement.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-03-c" name="p04-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Ask members to guess which answer their colleagues will approve.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-03-d" name="p04-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Ask the leader to announce the preferred answer before collecting facts.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-03-e" name="p04-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Replace factual discussion with a public loyalty vote.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> Investors buy after observing earlier purchases, although their private signals favor selling. Which additional evidence would most help distinguish an information cascade from independently justified optimism?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-04-a" name="p04-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> The fact that several investors buy at similar times.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-04-b" name="p04-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Check whether choices become insensitive to private signals.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-04-c" name="p04-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A list of the investors&#x27; favorite company names.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-04-d" name="p04-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> A claim that every buyer earned a later profit.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-04-e" name="p04-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> A price chart showing that the price increased.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> Two partners want continued cooperation, but accidental failures sometimes look like deliberate defection. Which rule best addresses this specific problem?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-05-a" name="p04-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Judge intentions solely from the worst observed outcome.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-05-b" name="p04-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Check evidence and allow repair before escalating punishment.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-05-c" name="p04-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Remove every consequence for deliberate exploitation.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-05-d" name="p04-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Treat every mistake as grounds for permanent retaliation.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-05-e" name="p04-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Stop recording the actions that caused disputes.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> A community introduces a small payment for an activity previously treated as a shared duty. Participation falls. Which follow-up best examines the proposed change in social meaning?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-06-a" name="p04-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Treat the participation decline as proof of lower physical ability.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-06-b" name="p04-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Compare only the income of people who continue participating.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-06-c" name="p04-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Infer that money reduces motivation in every setting.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-06-d" name="p04-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Randomize payments; compare reported obligation and subsequent participation.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-06-e" name="p04-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Increase payment while changing the activity and eligibility rules too.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> A trader believes a share is overpriced but expects enthusiastic buyers to push it higher before any correction. Why can waiting be strategically sensible?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-07-a" name="p04-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> A later correction guarantees that a short position survives all interim losses.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-07-b" name="p04-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> The path of others&#x27; demand affects the risk and timing of a corrective position.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-07-c" name="p04-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Believing in overpricing removes the need to forecast other traders.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-07-d" name="p04-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Expected short-run demand determines the share&#x27;s fundamental value by definition.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-07-e" name="p04-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Private valuation is equivalent to a publicly enforceable price cap.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> Employees publicly praise a policy. Anonymous surveys show most oppose it, expect colleagues to oppose it too, and fear the manager&#x27;s retaliation. Which diagnosis best fits this evidence?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-08-a" name="p04-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> A hidden-profile problem caused only by unshared technical facts</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-08-b" name="p04-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Pluralistic ignorance about colleagues&#x27; approval</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-08-c" name="p04-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Informational updating toward the manager&#x27;s superior evidence</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-08-d" name="p04-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Independent private endorsement of the policy</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-08-e" name="p04-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Public compliance under anticipated sanctions</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> In a symmetric coordination game, X pays 10 against X and 0 against Y; Y pays 7 against either action. Players maximize expected monetary payoff. Define risk dominance by the larger interval of beliefs making an action optimal. Which comparison is correct?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-09-a" name="p04-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> YY is the only Nash equilibrium.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-09-b" name="p04-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> XX is both payoff dominant and risk dominant.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-09-c" name="p04-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> YY is payoff dominant; XX is risk dominant.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-09-d" name="p04-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> XX is payoff dominant; YY is risk dominant.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-09-e" name="p04-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Both equilibria tie on risk dominance.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p04-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p04-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> Researchers want to test whether greater cash holdings increase bubbles in a laboratory market, where traders affect each other&#x27;s prices. Which randomization best isolates the market-level cash effect?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p04-10-a" name="p04-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Give experienced markets less cash and novice markets more.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p04-10-b" name="p04-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Increase cash and expected dividends together.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p04-10-c" name="p04-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Randomize multiple independent markets per cash level, holding asset supply, dividends, and rules fixed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p04-10-d" name="p04-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Randomize half the traders within each market and compare their purchase prices.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p04-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p04-10-e" name="p04-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Compare only markets selected because prices rose strongly.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p04-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>

<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p04"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p04-01"><h3>Question 1: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Adverse selection; moral hazard <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The first concerns hidden pre-contract characteristics; the second hidden post-contract action.</dd>
<dt>B. Coordination failure; payoff dominance <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>These terms do not identify the hidden-quality and hidden-effort problems.</dd>
<dt>C. Reciprocity; conditional cooperation <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>These preference patterns are distinct from the information structure.</dd>
<dt>D. Moral hazard; adverse selection <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses the timing and objects of private information.</dd>
<dt>E. Risk dominance; common knowledge <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Neither private fact is common knowledge, and no equilibrium selection is described.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.html">Chapter 23</a> · <a href="../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.html">Chapter 27</a>. <a href="#p04-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p04-02"><h3>Question 2: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. A ranking rewarding only superiority over the other team <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This strengthens intergroup competition.</dd>
<dt>B. Separate tasks with no need for interteam contact <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Separation provides no shared cooperative purpose.</dd>
<dt>C. A reminder that all members of each team think alike <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reinforces an unsupported group stereotype.</dd>
<dt>D. A shared task requiring contributions from both teams to succeed <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A superordinate goal can make cooperation across the boundary relevant.</dd>
<dt>E. More resources for the existing within-team competition <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This does not address the cross-team boundary.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.html">Chapter 25</a> · <a href="../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.html">Chapter 29</a>. <a href="#p04-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p04-03"><h3>Question 3: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Collect independent evidence privately, then discuss it under explicit protection for dissent. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>This surfaces unshared facts while reducing the identity and social cost of challenge.</dd>
<dt>B. Record only the final unanimous statement. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A consensus record can hide both missing facts and inhibited doubts.</dd>
<dt>C. Ask members to guess which answer their colleagues will approve. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This redirects attention toward anticipated social acceptance.</dd>
<dt>D. Ask the leader to announce the preferred answer before collecting facts. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This increases pressure before independent information is elicited.</dd>
<dt>E. Replace factual discussion with a public loyalty vote. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>That conflates allegiance with evidence.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/26-social-norms-and-conformity.html">Chapter 26</a> · <a href="../chapters/28-social-influence.html">Chapter 28</a> · <a href="../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.html">Chapter 29</a>. <a href="#p04-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p04-04"><h3>Question 4: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. The fact that several investors buy at similar times. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Correlated choices can also reflect common independent evidence.</dd>
<dt>B. Check whether choices become insensitive to private signals. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A cascade involves following actions despite private information.</dd>
<dt>C. A list of the investors&#x27; favorite company names. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Liking is not evidence about use of private signals.</dd>
<dt>D. A claim that every buyer earned a later profit. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Later outcomes do not establish how the original decisions used information.</dd>
<dt>E. A price chart showing that the price increased. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A price increase alone does not identify the mechanism.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/26-social-norms-and-conformity.html">Chapter 26</a> · <a href="../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.html">Chapter 27</a>. <a href="#p04-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p04-05"><h3>Question 5: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Judge intentions solely from the worst observed outcome. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Outcome severity alone does not distinguish accident from defection.</dd>
<dt>B. Check evidence and allow repair before escalating punishment. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A repair process can preserve cooperation when noisy actions are misread.</dd>
<dt>C. Remove every consequence for deliberate exploitation. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This weakens deterrence without specifically distinguishing mistakes.</dd>
<dt>D. Treat every mistake as grounds for permanent retaliation. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Noise can then trigger destructive escalation.</dd>
<dt>E. Stop recording the actions that caused disputes. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Missing records make diagnosis and repair harder.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.html">Chapter 23</a> · <a href="../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.html">Chapter 25</a>. <a href="#p04-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p04-06"><h3>Question 6: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Treat the participation decline as proof of lower physical ability. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Ability is not the stated mechanism.</dd>
<dt>B. Compare only the income of people who continue participating. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Post-treatment selection omits those whose participation changed.</dd>
<dt>C. Infer that money reduces motivation in every setting. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>One pattern does not support that generalization.</dd>
<dt>D. Randomize payments; compare reported obligation and subsequent participation. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>With the task, eligibility, and period fixed, this tests parallel changes in meaning and behavior; it does not identify obligation as the causal mediator.</dd>
<dt>E. Increase payment while changing the activity and eligibility rules too. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Multiple changes make interpretation difficult.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.html">Chapter 25</a> · <a href="../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.html">Chapter 29</a>. <a href="#p04-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p04-07"><h3>Question 7: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. A later correction guarantees that a short position survives all interim losses. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Funding and margin constraints can force early closure.</dd>
<dt>B. The path of others&#x27; demand affects the risk and timing of a corrective position. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Fundamental disagreement does not eliminate interim losses or funding constraints.</dd>
<dt>C. Believing in overpricing removes the need to forecast other traders. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Interim prices still depend on others&#x27; actions.</dd>
<dt>D. Expected short-run demand determines the share&#x27;s fundamental value by definition. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Trading demand and discounted cash-flow value are distinct.</dd>
<dt>E. Private valuation is equivalent to a publicly enforceable price cap. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A belief does not impose market prices.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.html">Chapter 23</a> · <a href="../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.html">Chapter 27</a>. <a href="#p04-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p04-08"><h3>Question 8: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. A hidden-profile problem caused only by unshared technical facts <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The stated barrier is retaliation, not absent factual pooling.</dd>
<dt>B. Pluralistic ignorance about colleagues&#x27; approval <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Employees correctly expect colleagues to oppose the policy.</dd>
<dt>C. Informational updating toward the manager&#x27;s superior evidence <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The surveys retain private opposition and specify fear.</dd>
<dt>D. Independent private endorsement of the policy <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The anonymous responses show opposition.</dd>
<dt>E. Public compliance under anticipated sanctions <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Private attitudes and beliefs about peers agree; fear explains public praise.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/26-social-norms-and-conformity.html">Chapter 26</a> · <a href="../chapters/28-social-influence.html">Chapter 28</a> · <a href="../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.html">Chapter 29</a>. <a href="#p04-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p04-09"><h3>Question 9: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. YY is the only Nash equilibrium. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Against X, choosing X gives 10 rather than 7.</dd>
<dt>B. XX is both payoff dominant and risk dominant. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The higher coordinated payoff does not make X optimal for most beliefs.</dd>
<dt>C. YY is payoff dominant; XX is risk dominant. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses both comparisons.</dd>
<dt>D. XX is payoff dominant; YY is risk dominant. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>XX pays 10 each, but X is optimal only when P(X) ≥ 0.7, a smaller interval.</dd>
<dt>E. Both equilibria tie on risk dominance. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Their optimal-belief intervals have lengths 0.3 and 0.7.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.html">Chapter 23</a> · <a href="../chapters/24-coordination-and-focal-points.html">Chapter 24</a>. <a href="#p04-09">Back to question 9</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p04-10"><h3>Question 10: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Give experienced markets less cash and novice markets more. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Experience is then confounded with cash.</dd>
<dt>B. Increase cash and expected dividends together. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Both demand capacity and the valuation benchmark change.</dd>
<dt>C. Randomize multiple independent markets per cash level, holding asset supply, dividends, and rules fixed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Treatment applies to the interacting market, with comparable valuation benchmarks.</dd>
<dt>D. Randomize half the traders within each market and compare their purchase prices. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Traders share prices and influence one another; this does not isolate separate market regimes.</dd>
<dt>E. Compare only markets selected because prices rose strongly. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Selecting on the outcome biases the treatment comparison.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.html">Chapter 25</a> · <a href="../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.html">Chapter 27</a>. <a href="#p04-10">Back to question 10</a></p></li>
</ol></details></form>

Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p04-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** Before contracting, buyers offer a price based on average quality, causing high-quality sellers with privately known quality to withdraw. After signing and receiving payment, a seller can reduce unobserved effort, lowering the buyer's service quality. Which pair identifies the two information problems?

A) Adverse selection; moral hazard
B) Coordination failure; payoff dominance
C) Reciprocity; conditional cooperation
D) Moral hazard; adverse selection
E) Risk dominance; common knowledge

:::

::: {#p04-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** Two teams cooperate internally but resist sharing resources across teams. Which intervention most directly targets the narrow boundary of cooperation?

A) A ranking rewarding only superiority over the other team
B) Separate tasks with no need for interteam contact
C) A reminder that all members of each team think alike
D) A shared task requiring contributions from both teams to succeed
E) More resources for the existing within-team competition

:::

::: {#p04-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** Team members have unique evidence but fear that public disagreement will look disloyal. Which combined procedure most directly addresses both problems?

A) Collect independent evidence privately, then discuss it under explicit protection for dissent.
B) Record only the final unanimous statement.
C) Ask members to guess which answer their colleagues will approve.
D) Ask the leader to announce the preferred answer before collecting facts.
E) Replace factual discussion with a public loyalty vote.

:::

::: {#p04-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** Investors buy after observing earlier purchases, although their private signals favor selling. Which additional evidence would most help distinguish an information cascade from independently justified optimism?

A) The fact that several investors buy at similar times.
B) Check whether choices become insensitive to private signals.
C) A list of the investors' favorite company names.
D) A claim that every buyer earned a later profit.
E) A price chart showing that the price increased.

:::

::: {#p04-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** Two partners want continued cooperation, but accidental failures sometimes look like deliberate defection. Which rule best addresses this specific problem?

A) Judge intentions solely from the worst observed outcome.
B) Check evidence and allow repair before escalating punishment.
C) Remove every consequence for deliberate exploitation.
D) Treat every mistake as grounds for permanent retaliation.
E) Stop recording the actions that caused disputes.

:::

::: {#p04-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** A community introduces a small payment for an activity previously treated as a shared duty. Participation falls. Which follow-up best examines the proposed change in social meaning?

A) Treat the participation decline as proof of lower physical ability.
B) Compare only the income of people who continue participating.
C) Infer that money reduces motivation in every setting.
D) Randomize payments; compare reported obligation and subsequent participation.
E) Increase payment while changing the activity and eligibility rules too.

:::

::: {#p04-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** A trader believes a share is overpriced but expects enthusiastic buyers to push it higher before any correction. Why can waiting be strategically sensible?

A) A later correction guarantees that a short position survives all interim losses.
B) The path of others' demand affects the risk and timing of a corrective position.
C) Believing in overpricing removes the need to forecast other traders.
D) Expected short-run demand determines the share's fundamental value by definition.
E) Private valuation is equivalent to a publicly enforceable price cap.

:::

::: {#p04-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** Employees publicly praise a policy. Anonymous surveys show most oppose it, expect colleagues to oppose it too, and fear the manager's retaliation. Which diagnosis best fits this evidence?

A) A hidden-profile problem caused only by unshared technical facts
B) Pluralistic ignorance about colleagues' approval
C) Informational updating toward the manager's superior evidence
D) Independent private endorsement of the policy
E) Public compliance under anticipated sanctions

:::

::: {#p04-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** In a symmetric coordination game, X pays 10 against X and 0 against Y; Y pays 7 against either action. Players maximize expected monetary payoff. Define risk dominance by the larger interval of beliefs making an action optimal. Which comparison is correct?

A) YY is the only Nash equilibrium.
B) XX is both payoff dominant and risk dominant.
C) YY is payoff dominant; XX is risk dominant.
D) XX is payoff dominant; YY is risk dominant.
E) Both equilibria tie on risk dominance.

:::

::: {#p04-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** Researchers want to test whether greater cash holdings increase bubbles in a laboratory market, where traders affect each other's prices. Which randomization best isolates the market-level cash effect?

A) Give experienced markets less cash and novice markets more.
B) Increase cash and expected dividends together.
C) Randomize multiple independent markets per cash level, holding asset supply, dividends, and rules fixed.
D) Randomize half the traders within each market and compare their purchase prices.
E) Compare only markets selected because prices rose strongly.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-p04)

::: {#answers-p04 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: A.**

- **A. Adverse selection; moral hazard (Correct)** The first concerns hidden pre-contract characteristics; the second hidden post-contract action.
- **B. Coordination failure; payoff dominance (Incorrect)** These terms do not identify the hidden-quality and hidden-effort problems.
- **C. Reciprocity; conditional cooperation (Incorrect)** These preference patterns are distinct from the information structure.
- **D. Moral hazard; adverse selection (Incorrect)** This reverses the timing and objects of private information.
- **E. Risk dominance; common knowledge (Incorrect)** Neither private fact is common knowledge, and no equilibrium selection is described.

Review: [Chapter 23](../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.qmd) · [Chapter 27](../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p04-01).

**Question 2: D.**

- **A. A ranking rewarding only superiority over the other team (Incorrect)** This strengthens intergroup competition.
- **B. Separate tasks with no need for interteam contact (Incorrect)** Separation provides no shared cooperative purpose.
- **C. A reminder that all members of each team think alike (Incorrect)** This reinforces an unsupported group stereotype.
- **D. A shared task requiring contributions from both teams to succeed (Correct)** A superordinate goal can make cooperation across the boundary relevant.
- **E. More resources for the existing within-team competition (Incorrect)** This does not address the cross-team boundary.

Review: [Chapter 25](../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.qmd) · [Chapter 29](../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p04-02).

**Question 3: A.**

- **A. Collect independent evidence privately, then discuss it under explicit protection for dissent. (Correct)** This surfaces unshared facts while reducing the identity and social cost of challenge.
- **B. Record only the final unanimous statement. (Incorrect)** A consensus record can hide both missing facts and inhibited doubts.
- **C. Ask members to guess which answer their colleagues will approve. (Incorrect)** This redirects attention toward anticipated social acceptance.
- **D. Ask the leader to announce the preferred answer before collecting facts. (Incorrect)** This increases pressure before independent information is elicited.
- **E. Replace factual discussion with a public loyalty vote. (Incorrect)** That conflates allegiance with evidence.

Review: [Chapter 26](../chapters/26-social-norms-and-conformity.qmd) · [Chapter 28](../chapters/28-social-influence.qmd) · [Chapter 29](../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p04-03).

**Question 4: B.**

- **A. The fact that several investors buy at similar times. (Incorrect)** Correlated choices can also reflect common independent evidence.
- **B. Check whether choices become insensitive to private signals. (Correct)** A cascade involves following actions despite private information.
- **C. A list of the investors' favorite company names. (Incorrect)** Liking is not evidence about use of private signals.
- **D. A claim that every buyer earned a later profit. (Incorrect)** Later outcomes do not establish how the original decisions used information.
- **E. A price chart showing that the price increased. (Incorrect)** A price increase alone does not identify the mechanism.

Review: [Chapter 26](../chapters/26-social-norms-and-conformity.qmd) · [Chapter 27](../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p04-04).

**Question 5: B.**

- **A. Judge intentions solely from the worst observed outcome. (Incorrect)** Outcome severity alone does not distinguish accident from defection.
- **B. Check evidence and allow repair before escalating punishment. (Correct)** A repair process can preserve cooperation when noisy actions are misread.
- **C. Remove every consequence for deliberate exploitation. (Incorrect)** This weakens deterrence without specifically distinguishing mistakes.
- **D. Treat every mistake as grounds for permanent retaliation. (Incorrect)** Noise can then trigger destructive escalation.
- **E. Stop recording the actions that caused disputes. (Incorrect)** Missing records make diagnosis and repair harder.

Review: [Chapter 23](../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.qmd) · [Chapter 25](../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p04-05).

**Question 6: D.**

- **A. Treat the participation decline as proof of lower physical ability. (Incorrect)** Ability is not the stated mechanism.
- **B. Compare only the income of people who continue participating. (Incorrect)** Post-treatment selection omits those whose participation changed.
- **C. Infer that money reduces motivation in every setting. (Incorrect)** One pattern does not support that generalization.
- **D. Randomize payments; compare reported obligation and subsequent participation. (Correct)** With the task, eligibility, and period fixed, this tests parallel changes in meaning and behavior; it does not identify obligation as the causal mediator.
- **E. Increase payment while changing the activity and eligibility rules too. (Incorrect)** Multiple changes make interpretation difficult.

Review: [Chapter 25](../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.qmd) · [Chapter 29](../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p04-06).

**Question 7: B.**

- **A. A later correction guarantees that a short position survives all interim losses. (Incorrect)** Funding and margin constraints can force early closure.
- **B. The path of others' demand affects the risk and timing of a corrective position. (Correct)** Fundamental disagreement does not eliminate interim losses or funding constraints.
- **C. Believing in overpricing removes the need to forecast other traders. (Incorrect)** Interim prices still depend on others' actions.
- **D. Expected short-run demand determines the share's fundamental value by definition. (Incorrect)** Trading demand and discounted cash-flow value are distinct.
- **E. Private valuation is equivalent to a publicly enforceable price cap. (Incorrect)** A belief does not impose market prices.

Review: [Chapter 23](../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.qmd) · [Chapter 27](../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p04-07).

**Question 8: E.**

- **A. A hidden-profile problem caused only by unshared technical facts (Incorrect)** The stated barrier is retaliation, not absent factual pooling.
- **B. Pluralistic ignorance about colleagues' approval (Incorrect)** Employees correctly expect colleagues to oppose the policy.
- **C. Informational updating toward the manager's superior evidence (Incorrect)** The surveys retain private opposition and specify fear.
- **D. Independent private endorsement of the policy (Incorrect)** The anonymous responses show opposition.
- **E. Public compliance under anticipated sanctions (Correct)** Private attitudes and beliefs about peers agree; fear explains public praise.

Review: [Chapter 26](../chapters/26-social-norms-and-conformity.qmd) · [Chapter 28](../chapters/28-social-influence.qmd) · [Chapter 29](../chapters/29-culture-and-identity.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p04-08).

**Question 9: D.**

- **A. YY is the only Nash equilibrium. (Incorrect)** Against X, choosing X gives 10 rather than 7.
- **B. XX is both payoff dominant and risk dominant. (Incorrect)** The higher coordinated payoff does not make X optimal for most beliefs.
- **C. YY is payoff dominant; XX is risk dominant. (Incorrect)** This reverses both comparisons.
- **D. XX is payoff dominant; YY is risk dominant. (Correct)** XX pays 10 each, but X is optimal only when P(X) ≥ 0.7, a smaller interval.
- **E. Both equilibria tie on risk dominance. (Incorrect)** Their optimal-belief intervals have lengths 0.3 and 0.7.

Review: [Chapter 23](../chapters/23-strategic-interdependence.qmd) · [Chapter 24](../chapters/24-coordination-and-focal-points.qmd). [Back to question 9](#p04-09).

**Question 10: C.**

- **A. Give experienced markets less cash and novice markets more. (Incorrect)** Experience is then confounded with cash.
- **B. Increase cash and expected dividends together. (Incorrect)** Both demand capacity and the valuation benchmark change.
- **C. Randomize multiple independent markets per cash level, holding asset supply, dividends, and rules fixed. (Correct)** Treatment applies to the interacting market, with comparable valuation benchmarks.
- **D. Randomize half the traders within each market and compare their purchase prices. (Incorrect)** Traders share prices and influence one another; this does not isolate separate market regimes.
- **E. Compare only markets selected because prices rose strongly. (Incorrect)** Selecting on the outcome biases the treatment comparison.

Review: [Chapter 25](../chapters/25-cooperation-and-social-preferences.qmd) · [Chapter 27](../chapters/27-markets-mispricing-and-bubbles.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p04-10).

:::
